The assay measures cytopathic effect (CPE) reduction, so cytotoxic compounds that kill host cells will appear inactive or be excluded.

Because this is a whole-cell phenotypic assay rather than a target-specific biochemical assay, the molecular features that drive activity are more diverse. Active compounds in this screen include repurposed drugs (e.g., remdesivir — an RdRp inhibitor, hydroxychloroquine — a lysosomotropic agent, lopinavir — an HIV protease inhibitor) as well as novel hits from diverse chemical libraries. Functional groups associated with known antiviral mechanisms — nucleoside/nucleotide analogues for RdRp inhibition, peptidomimetic groups for protease inhibition, cationic amphiphilic structures for lysosomotropic accumulation. Adequate aqueous solubility for testing at effective concentrations.

Features arguing against activity: very large, poorly cell-permeable molecules (MW > 800, TPSA > 150 Å²) that cannot reach intracellular targets. Highly lipophilic compounds (logP > 6) with poor solubility. Reactive or cytotoxic compounds — the CPE-reduction assay requires that the compound be non-toxic to host cells at the active concentration.
